articles.title: The UFC is hard to like. Kayla Harrison shows why it’s harder to dismiss | Bryan Armen Graham
articles.summary: Dana White’s company squeezes fighters, bullies journalists and toadies up to Trump. But it has also given neglected Olympians a path to money and fame that didn’t exist before it. If you don’t like what is being said, change the conversation.
body: Trump’s turn to White’s trademark bluster was a simple enough gambit to parse. In 2024, he rode the manosphere to an astonishing 63% backing among young white men, with White name-checking Joe Rogan, Theo Von, Adin Ross and the Nelk Boys from the victory podium like the heterodox heirs to Bill Buckley. Two years later, that support had cratered by 20 points in the midterms: the political equivalent of a 10-8 round. Suddenly, the prospect of White as some cauliflower-eared CJ Cregg seemed less like comic relief than a panicked attempt to inject a cycle of synthetic testosterone into Maga’s increasingly low-energy movement.

The UFC was hardly about to abandon its oldest instincts. From its earliest days as a pay-per-view curiosity derided as “human cockfighting”, it has thrived on thumbing its nose at polite liberal consensus. Nowhere did the establishment resist more fiercely than here in New York, which banned professional MMA in 1997 and held out until March 2016 as the 50th and final US state to legalize it – and even then only after Democratic assembly members called it “a terrible, nasty, violent sport” and “a sad day” before reluctantly giving it the green light.
points: Dana White’s company squeezes fighters, bullies journalists and toadies up to Trump.
But it has also given neglected Olympians a path to money and fame that didn’t exist before it.

articles.title: Cricket Australia admits it is ‘very unlikely’ players will ever reach agreement on sandpapergate
articles.summary: Bowler Chadd Sayers rejects Pat Cummins’ view on ball tampering. Governing body ‘respects right’ of players sharing their versions. Cricket Australia admits there is little hope of reaching agreement on the events of the sandpaper ball-tampering incident, as divisions deepen between the players who…
body: The former Australia bowler Chadd Sayers on Sunday said he was confident “everyone” in the Australian Test side knew of the ball-tampering plan, backing Usman Khawaja’s version of what happened.

Sayers, a member of the touring party for the 2018 series, also rejected Pat Cummins’ claim that there was no team meeting to discuss collective responsibility and took aim at the Australian captain for getting “personal” with Khawaja in his press conference on the scandal.

“I’m comfortable sitting here … that I believe that everyone in that side knew what was going on and what was being used,” Sayers told SEN radio on Sunday. “I’m not taking sides. I’m neutral in all this … I’m just trying to tell my side of the story and what I believe happened.”

Cricket Australia responded to the comments later on Sunday. “We respect the right of those in South Africa in 2018 to share their version of what they believe happened on that tour,” a spokesperson said.

articles.title: Banton pushes case and bowlers sparkle for inconsistent England
articles.summary: Tom Banton scores a century and Sonny Baker and Gus Atkinson impress with the ball as England's wildly inconsistent one-day team hammer Australia.
body: Tom Banton scored a century and Sonny Baker and Gus Atkinson impressed with the ball as England's wildly inconsistent one-day team hammered Australia to set up a series decider.
Banton scored a fine 121 – pushing his case for selection further with a second ODI hundred – in England's 355-6.
After being knocked over for 131 two days ago in Perth, England's total was their highest in one-day internationals in Australia.

And then their bowlers, who failed to defend 430 against Sri Lanka last month and were undone by an improbable last-wicket partnership against Pakistan, reduced Australia to 29-4 inside seven overs and easily closed out a 135-run victory.

articles.title: Terry Butcher: ‘I’ve learned to live with the Hand of God goal better’
articles.summary: The former England centre-back answers your questions on Diego Maradona, Bobby Robson and on staying in strange places. “Have you made up all these on your own?” asks Terry Butcher, sitting in a London office in the week he is presented with his England legacy cap.
body: Did Maradona ever admit to the “Hand of God”? Butcher found himself in the post-match doping-control room alongside his nemesis at the Azteca in 1986. “I tapped my head, then my hand, and then he tapped his head,” Butcher says. “He didn’t admit to it because, if he had, I’d have been right across that room.”
The highs and lows of Sir Bobby Robson’s remarkable England tenure are chronicled in a new book co-written by Butcher: Almost Immortal: When Bobby Robson’s England Gripped The Nation.

I’ve actually stayed in that room as well. Stu has told us what it was like for him and I have to say it wasn’t great for me either. I’m staring up looking at me with a bloodied head and thinking: “Oh my God, this has followed me around.” At least when you close your eyes and sleep you don’t have to see it, but I’m sorry he had to stay there.

articles.title: AFC Wimbledon, a failed £87m investment bid and the challenge for fan ownership
articles.summary: Clubs with wealthy proprietors can maintain a loss-making operation but things can be more complex when the supporters carry the can. When you walk up from Haydons Road train station to Plough Lane there is a blue AFC Wimbledon billboard that reads “Fan owned football”, directly opposite the site…
body: AFC Wimbledon are one of only two majority fan-owned clubs in the EFL – along with Exeter City – but that makes running a loss-making operation, as 94% of teams in England’s top five tiers are doing according to the State of the Game report, even more challenging. “In other clubs, the owner just puts their hand in their pocket, produces cash,” said Hannah Kitcher, who has been a member of the Dons Trust Board (DTB), which runs AFC Wimbledon, for seven years. “It’s harder when the owners are fans – you can only go to them so many times.”

Kitcher was speaking before kick-off in Saturday’s League One game at home to a Blackpool side dealing with a suspected norovirus outbreak in their squad. A superb arrowed strike from Alistair Smith and some vital late saves from Nathan Bishop ended Wimbledon’s winless run of 10 matches in all competitions. The 1-0 victory moved Johnnie Jackson’s side four points clear of the relegation zone and put a positive spin on a week that started with the fallout from the withdrawal of £87m of proposed investment, leaving the club’s finances even tighter.

articles.title: England level ODI series with Australia as Banton and Atkinson fire
articles.summary: Tom Banton's second ODI hundred and Gus Atkinson's sizzling new-ball burst saw England thump Australia by 135 runs in Adelaide and set up a series decider in Hobart on Wednesday.
body: A touring side rolled for 131 in Friday's opener at Perth posted their highest ODI total in Australia, with a score of 355-6 underpinned by Banton's 121 from 99 balls and featuring fifties for Jordan Cox (67 off 49), Joe Root (62 off 68) and Will Jacks (54no off 40).

England lost their fourth wicket in the 35th over - Banton holing out immediately after back-to-back sixes - whereas Australia lost their fourth at the end of the seventh with just 29 runs on the board, before being dismissed for 220 in 44.3 overs with Atkinson claiming 4-28.

The ODI finale at Ninja Stadium in Tasmania next week (3.30am start UK on Wednesday) is now winner-takes-all, ahead of the sides moving on to a five-match T20 international series, starting at the Melbourne Cricket Ground next Saturday (8.15am UK time).

articles.title: Australia brush off New Zealand to win fourth straight Rugby League World Cup
articles.summary: Jack Bostock and Liam Martin both starred as Australia swept away New Zealand 32-12 in the men's Rugby League World Cup final to be crowned world champions for the fourth time in a row.
body: The Kangaroos wasted no time in getting on the scoreboard, with Martin driving over inside three minutes.
X-factor full-back Reece Walsh was once again in emphatic form, tearing apart the Kiwi defence as his side romped to score four first-half tries.
Bostock had another inside 20 minutes before Bradman Best crashed over 10 minutes before half-time.
Martin and Tom Trbojevic bookended tries either side of the interval, before Isaiah Papali'i got one back for New Zealand.

articles.summary: Australia bowler Chadd Sayers says he helped take sandpaper from the field in the match prior to the Cape Town Test and backs Usman Khawaja's recollection over Pat Cummins'.
body: Sayers, 39, was 12th man during the second Test of the 2018 series against South Africa in Gqeberha, previously known as Port Elizabeth, and backed the claim from Khawaja's book that sandpaper was also used there.
"That wasn't planned or anything. It was a wicket or drinks break after tea."

Sayers also said there was a "60 to 90-minute" meeting in the Australia dressing room after Bancroft had been caught using sandpaper in Cape Town, in which players discussed taking collective responsibility - something Khawaja claims but Cummins said he did not remember in his extraordinary news conference on Friday.
"I am comfortable sitting here that I believe everyone in that side knew what was going on and what was being used," said Sayers, whose one Test was the final match of that series.

articles.title: Ruthless Australia win record fourth Women's World Cup
articles.summary: Australia blow New Zealand away in the first half, with a hat-trick for Jaime Chapman, to win 34-10 in Brisbane and clinch a record fourth World Cup.
body: Jaime Chapman's grin after acrobatically diving over in the corner said it all. Her second try of the match and Australia's third – the World Cup final put to bed inside 15 minutes.
The red-hot Australian winning machine blew New Zealand away in the first half as they cantered to a record fourth World Cup title - and fourth in a row - with a 34-10 victory in Brisbane.

Making light work of the blistering conditions, which necessitated a drinks break in either half and an extended interval, the Jillaroos ran in six tries to the Kiwi Ferns' one in the opening 35 minutes, including an initial burst of 24 unanswered points and a hat-trick for Chapman.

Record books were consulted at the break, with Australia on course to challenge New Zealand's 58-0 winning margin from the 2003 final. But the two sides neutralised one another during the second period, New Zealand maintaining their record of not conceding after the break at this tournament - and bagging a consolation try - albeit with Australia long out of sight.

articles.title: Erling Haaland snaps back at questions on Man City charges
articles.summary: Erling Haaland says he is "incredibly happy" at Manchester City, insisting his focus remains on performing rather than potential sanctions against the club. City have launched an appeal having been found guilty of more than 100 breaches of the Premier League ’s financial regulations.
body: Haaland addressed the case following Norway’s 3-1 Nations League win over Wales in Oslo on Saturday night, where he registered his 66th goal in 60 international appearances.
“This is a question I struggle to answer, because it’s a legal battle between the Premier League and Manchester City,” Haaland told Norwegian broadcaster TV2.
“Am I supposed to answer that? I don’t really know. It’s a difficult question to answer when I don’t know that much about it.
“To be completely honest, I’m focused on trying to perform for Manchester City. A club I signed a five-year deal with in 2022, and a new nine-and-a-half-year deal in late 2024.
